At a cost of about $25,000 a year, the government could pay the surtax imposed upon the evaporated apple products and relieve the Canadian industry. This would do almost more than anything else, as I have already suggested, to assist the farmer in getting rid of the apples that otherwise would be lost. I cannot speak too highly of the advantage of the evaporator to the farmer.
I believe that advantage is as great as that afforded by the canneries. I believe the government would be wise in deciding to assist the people engaged in this bust ness.
, Mr. M. S. SCHELL (South Oxford). It is very pleasing to see the spirit in which this subject has been debated, for it is so seldom that we find both sides of the House agreeing so thoroughly on any matter as to-day. We know that the work of the fruit inspectors has been most helpful to the apple industry as well as to the industry of growing small fruit. I do not propose to quote, as I might quote at length from different sources, to show how the work that has been done by the inspectors since they were appointed in 1901 is regarded. The fact that our friends of the opposition are asking for an increase m the number of inspectors is the clearest proof that good work has been done. I have a very high appreciation of this trade, its growth and possibilities. I agree heartily with the hon. member for Yale-Oariboo concerning the possibilities of the apple industry-and I suppose the same applies to small fruits-in the province of British Columbia. We feel that there are as great possibilities in the province of Ontario. We know that the fruit of British Columbia is of very fine quality very handsome, perhaps even more so than the Ontario fruit or that of Nova Scotia But we know that it is not finer in quality Ontario, I think, produces the best ali round apples, perhaps not as fine in appearance, but for flavour, for texture, and for keeping quality, I do not think there is any part of the Dominion of Canada tnat produces finer apples, or possibly as 107
good. ^ The possibilities of development in Ontario are very great, yet I am sorry to say we have been making but very little progress of late years. The number of new orchards that are being set out is very small, comparatively speaking; the older orchards we have are not producing the quality of fruit that they should produce, and there is something lacking with this industry. Now, I do not blame the Dominion government, I do not blame the Ontario government, either one of them entirely;
kiplr perhaps the fault lies primarily at the door of the producer, at the door of the grower.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The packer?

No, not the packer, you have to go far behind the packer to find the root of the trouble. If we are going to put this industry where it should be, and if we are going to have our inspectors do their work satisfactorily in the future, we have got to produce a better quality of fruit. The inspectors have done about all they can do, except as a deterrent in future. The educational work has demonstrated that our fruit has to be put up according to a certain standard, and packers buyers and dealers Understand that. But until we get a better quality of fruit a more uniform quality, there will always be a difficulty in the enforcement of the Fruit Marks Act, and our growers will not obtain the^ value that they should obtain from their orchards.
I think that in the first place more educational work should be done. The farmers already know something of it from reading in the newspapers, and from the example of their neighbours in spraying their orchards and taking proper care of them. But as a rule, our farmers have not gone systematically into the work of spraying and caring for their orchards as they should do. I believe the provincial government of Ontario, assisted by the Dominion government, should take up this work more energetically in the way of imparting education, instruction, and making demonstrations with a view of putting this in-"usj'ry on a better footing. I understand that the provincial government of British Columbia have taken a very strong stand in relation to their fruit industries, and I think they are far in advance of us in the province of Ontario-and I am now speaking particularly for that province. It is the provincial government of Ontario that have primarily the charge of the educational institutions, and it is their duty to do more in the way of sending out inspectors and instructors. If the apple industry, the fruit industry, of that province were properly handled, instead of exporting one million barrels of apples, out of the ten million or fifteen million we produce in that prov-
What do you think of the freight rates to the west?

I think they are too high and I think that the railway companies of this country should give us better rates. Especially is it unfair that when the fruit gets to Winnipeg local rates prevail from Winnipeg to western points. That is an absolutely unfair condition that I think our Board of Railway Commissioners should take up and deal with. We should have a through rate to Calgary, Edmonton, Brandon or Regina, as well as to Winnipeg, and I think it is an absolutely unfair condition that is maintained to the detriment of the shippers of Ontario fruit. The rate is high anyway, and I think we are entitled to a through rate just as much as we would be in shipping any other commodity. I hope that this government, operating in connection with the government of Ontario and, if necessary, with the government of Nova Scotia, if their system is not what it should be, as well as with the government of British Columbia, will take hold of this industry and spend money upon it. Every dollar they spend they will get back ten times over as the result of better educative work. I do not know of any industry in which there are greater possibilities of development. I do not know any way in which the government can spend money and receive a better return. Instead of having complaints about poor fruit and inspectors not always giving satisfaction either to the shippers or the buyers, if we get the fruit right there will be no difficulty about the inspection, and if we had the clean fruit they have in British Columbia and in some of the western states there would not be much difficulty about inspection. -There the fruit is comparatively clean. They have not the scab and coddling moth to the same extent that we have in Ontario. By solving the question of the production of a good quality of fruit at home we will rid ourselves of the difficulty, annoyance and heart burnings in connection with poor fruit that we sometimes see put up and shipped to the markets that should never leave our own orchards except to go the evaporator or cider mill.

Mr. Speaker, I have only a word to add to what has been said. I am more than pleased that this subject has come up to-day. This is the fruit grower's day. We have sometimes a lawyers' day, we have always a political partisans' day and during the last few years I believe we have had, once in each session, a doctors' day. I am very glad therefore that to-day we have a fruit growers' day. I think that much good will come of it. I am very glad that this question has come up. It is one in which I am personally deeply interested, coming from 1071
a country where fruit growing is one of our chief industries, where fruit growing is one of our most paying industries, where the apple tree is indigenous to the soil, [DOT]where it will grow wild in the fence corners alongside of the morning glories and the wild roses, where you can scent the apple blossoms for a hundred miles in one direction without losing sight of the blooms all the way. It is one of our paying industries. Apple growing in Nova Scotia is as good as owning bank stock even if bank stock is good. My hon. friend (Mr. Schell) who has been telling us about the superior fruit, the unapproachable fruit of Ontario, I am sorry to say, wound up with a hard luck tale about bad fruit, miserable, scabby fruit, wormy fruit, unintelligently cultivated and unintelligently packed. I would advise our friend to send his fruit growers either to British Columbia or down to Nova Scotia to get some lessons in intelligent fruit growing and intelligent and honest packing. I am also glad that this question has come up because it has developed that the only fault which the Fruit Marks Act has is that there are not enough inspectors. I remember that not very long ago, at least one of the voices that was singing the praises of this Act to-day and finding no fault with it at all, was criticising this Act very energetically and very earnestly, and I also remember that it was attacked very bitterly. But the hon. gentleman who was then criticising the Act declares to-day that the only fault to be found with it is that there are not enough inspectors. The outfit of inspectors necessary to examine our apple crop would be something like the outfit of surgical instruments that a surgeon would need. It could not be complete. I presume the inspectors were appointed to look after four classes of the people in the fruit business-the ignorant grower, the ignorant packer, the careless packer and the dishonest packer. The want of education, I think, is one thing that has made the inspector necessary at all. If our people were sufficiently educated in the art and skill of growing apples properly, of growing them for their own profit, of growing them in a businesslike way, I think we would have very little trouble about the quantity of inspectors. In so far as Nova Scotia is concerned I have nothing but good words to say for the Fruit Marks Act'. We have not many inspectors there, not as many as would like to be appointed, but I think possibly that at the present time we have about all that are necessary. We exported from the port of Halifax last year between 600,000 and 700,000 barrels of apples and so intelligently is the fruit grown and so honestly is it packed that the two or three inspectors that are employed in Nova Scotia, one of whom is at the port of Halifax, are all that are

necessary. I have it on the authority of the chief inspector that while in some cases fruit packers are being fined every year, the fact is that dishonest fruit packing is growing less and less all the time. As in other businesses, so in the fruit growing business, education and intelligence are necessary, and if my hon. friend from Ontario inquires into the sad situation he paints he will find that the trouble in Ontario is that while the soil is fit and the conditions favourable the people are not growing the fruit intelligently. The hon. gentleman told us that $300 per acre was paid for land, and he seems to consider that an enormous sum. Let me tell him that down where I come from you cannot buy an acre of orchard for $300.
The statement was that the fruit itself was sold at $300 per acre.

I could mention an orchard in my district on which last year the fruit sold for $4,000. However, that makes very little difference, for what I was getting at was the importance of intelligence in growing fruit. The fruit growers in my section of the country are educated and intelligent men and we have B.A's. and M. A's., graduates of our colleges, engaged in the industry. The 'result is that fruit growing in Nova Scotia is not only a paying business now, but that year after year we find our export of fruit growing larger and the quality of the apples getting better. Perhaps in some sections of the country where fruit is not so intelligently grown and where perhaps it is a little more dishonestly packed there may be more inspectors required, but in Nova Scotia we have no fault whatever to find with the Act and indeed we think it has proved itself to be a very great benefit to the industry.

I have listened with much interest to the statements made by hon. gentlemen as to the many evils that confront us in the fruit growing industry, but as they have offered no remedy I trust I may be pardoned for making a suggestion which I think will bring about a cure for these evils. We realize that all through Canada qj>ples and oranges are of the same value. I had occasion to state in the House recently that last fall apples in my locality sold for from 8 cents to 25 cents per 100 pounds, and I have before me a report of the market in Great Britain from which it will be seen that at the same time apples sold there for as low as one shilling per barrel. In my belief the remedy that would enable the apple crop to be marketed in a manner so as to bring to the growers the greatest return would be to introduce proper cold storage facilities nearer the points where the apples are produced. Until that is done Mr. BLACK.
I do not think the apple crop can be made to bring to the growers that return which it ought to bring.
That is what we do.

I am very glad to hear it. We all know what a benefit the cold storage system has been to the cheese industry and my suggestion is that the Minister of Agriculture should adopt similar methods in relation to the apple growing industry, and that educational stations should be established so as to teach the growers how to produce the best crop and how to market it in the best condition when it is produced. I urge this view of the case upon the Minister of Agriculture and I trust he will take steps in that direction.

I was somewhat amused at the speech of the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Schell), because, while he told us in one breath that transportation had reached a high state of perfection, in the next breath he said that the facilities for transportation to Winnipeg and the west were wretched, that the freight rates were exorbitant and that the fruit was not well handled.
I did not say anything about the handling of the fruit; I only spoke about the question of rates.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Schell) told us that we had the best system of cold storage in the world, but if that be so, _ how is it that so many shipments of fruit to England last year have been reported as being in bad condition when they arrived at their destination. I think that could be minimized greatly had we better cold storage and better care of the fruit on the voyage. The hon. gentleman blamed the Ontario government for not doing as much as he thought they ought to do in this direction, but I think that with him it depends a good deal on whose ox is gored. He thought the federal government was doing everything all right but of course he thought the Ontario government was doing everything all wrong. My belief is that both governments might do more than they have done, and, while we may provide cold storage and proper transportation we must also remember that proper culture of the fruit is a most important thing. There is something needed beyond all that, and fhat is the proper cultivation of the ground and its proper fertilization. Compare our orchards here with those in southern California. In the latter you would not see a blade of grass growing, they are practically cultivated all the time. The cultivation of the soil is not only looked after but the increase of moisture, and all that is needed as well as spraying and other devices. My hon. friend

from Oxford (Mr. Schell) gave as an instance of what might be accomplished in the fruit line, what has been done in the manufacture and export of cheese. No doubt that is the case, but was the excellent work done in the cheese line all done by government? Not at all. It was done by the united efforts of the governments and the cheese men themselves. For years back, in the county my hon. friend represents, the cheese manufacturers have had their own men in the field lecturing and instructing, and that, combined with the work done by the government, helped to accomplish what has been attained in that business. It was owing to the united efforts of the people belonging to the cheese associations and of both the federal and local governments that the trade in that commodity was so much improved. If we desire to accomplish something similar in the fruit business, we shall have to do it largely on the same lines. Last year we exported 1,600,000 barrels of apples, which must be only a small fraction of all that we grew and that we might have exported if the prices realized paid the expense. Besides we exported 6,000,000 pounds of evaporated apples. I do not know at what price these are sold elsewhere when picked, but in my county they sold at 25 cents a hundred during last year. That was a very small price, but the apples taken to the evaporator are not of a quality which would do for barrelling. They were practically the product of the orchard not fit for other markets, and although sold at inferior prices, if you add these prices to those obtained for the good exportable apples, you have a good average. To my mind what is required is a more rigid inspection and more inspections. I agree with the hon. minister that it would be altogether too much paternalism to send inspectors into every orchard to show the people how to pack their apples. That they ought to learn themselves, and it is something which their own innate honesty ought to dictate to them. But the apples should be examined periodically to see if packed and graded according to; law, and to punish those individuals who violate the law and in that way destroy the reputation of Canadian goods. We want more inspectors and we require a better system of cold storage. We want cold storage places in which to keep the apples and then have cold storage transportation both in the cars and on the steamers. We also require men at every port to look after their loading and unloading, to see that they are not exposed, to see that they are kept in proper condition, and when they reach their port of destination to see that they are taken charge of and put into cold storage again until they are sold. In addition to that, we require better freight
rates. Our freight rates are entirely too high, both ocean and railway. They take away a portion of the profit which otherwise would go to the exporters and the growers of the fruit. When these things are done, we shall have better results. We also ought to make greater efforts to find out markets abroad. In that way we could do something which would enure to the benefit of our fruit growers and exporters. In addition we should have an increase in the duty upon imported fruit so as to keep a lot of foreign fruit out of the Canadian market. We are entitled to have our own markets for our own people. Should the government operate along these lines, they will be doing something which cannot fail to benefit the trade generally.

I have been much interested in the discussion we have had on the Fruit Marks Act and its administration, and I am glad to find that the department has been endorsed all along the line for the good results accruing from the Fruit Marks Act and its administration. The only complaint apparently seems to be that there are scarcely enough inspectors, and scarcely enough work done along the line of inspection, that the packers are not watched quite close enough. The very satisfactory explanation of the work of the department given by the hon. Minister of Agriculture renders it entirely unnecessary on my part to supplement it, but I shall take the liberty of drawing attention to one phase of the case which has come to my notice in the way of local observation. The packers and shippers, as a rule, so far as one can judge at home, who complain most loudly of the lack of effort on the part of the department and of the infraction of the law by others are generally the greatest sinners themselves. The large shippers are constantly complaining in order to induce the inspectors to be exceedingly hard on the smaller packers and shippers and in that way draw attention away from the quality of their own work. But so far as 1 can observe, the greatest infractions of the Act are committed by the packers and buyers who purchase by the orchard rather than by the barrel. When they buy by the orchard, they get the whole product, and they consider it most profitable to take everything which they can have the slightest chance of selling. Whereas when they buy by the barrel, _ they are far more cautious, the inspection is far more rigid, and consequently the result is much better. If I could venture to offer a word of suggestion or caution, it would be that the department should impress on its inspectors the _ advisability of paying rather most of their attention to those localities where the practice is to buy the orchards outright. I am not suggesting that that is not a satisfactory and simple

way of adjusting between the grower and the packer and shipper, but, so far as my observation goes, that is where the greatest mischief results. Not that the other methods are entirely satisfactory by any means, but this method is open to a great deal of abuse. I am sure that we are all pleased to have the assurance of the hon. minister that if any more inspectors be required, even though the appropriation be exhausted, he will not hesitate to appoint them, and if he does the House will have still greater confidence in him and his administration of the department, even though there be an overdraft. While the remarks and suggestions in this House have been largely with reference to the watching of the transhipping of the 'fruit and of the operations of the packers, I think the idea of the large packers and shippers in each locality is to get the government inspectors to do the work of inspecting the small packers and shippers from whom they buy, an expense and duty which should fall on the large packers themselves as a business transaction. While I agree with and am glad to endorse the Department of Agriculture in going to the extra expense proposed, it is just a question how far the department, in the public interest, should be encouraged to devote its energies to looking after the small packers for the benefit of the large packers and shippers.
We can all endorse most heartily the proposition to provide increased cold storage accommodation, especially in the vicinity of fruit growing centres, and I am satisfied that this matter is, as we were assured, engaging the consideration of the department and that we may anticipate a further improvement at an early date. I would again suggest that the department have their inspectors watch moTe closely the packers who are in the habit of buying apples on the trees and to whose interest it is to pack as many apples as they can.

speechtext:
House in committee on Bill (No. 94) respecting the Cedar Rapids Manufacturing & Power Company.-Mr. Boyer
On section 1-Expropriation powers1-' time extended.

subtopic: CEDAR RAPIDS MANUFACTURING AND POWER COMPANY.
speechtext: It does not seem to me that we ought to pass this Bill in the shape in which it appears before us. A charter was granted to this company in 1904 as a power company in connection with the Cedar Rapids on the St. Lawrence river. They were given until this year to make use of certain expropriation powers that were given them. Now, they come back and ask us to extend these expropriation powers until 1914. Their charter gives them very large powers with regard to using the water at Cedar Rapids. If they wish to develop the water-power, they ought to do it, and should not come here to ask us to extend these rights for five years. That would mean that the development of this power might be tied up for that length of time, even though for merely speculative purposes. We ought not to grant expropriation powers extending over so many years unless the parties have shown their good faith, and have shown that they intend to go on with the work.

speakeroldname: Hon. WM. PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works).
subtopic: CEDAR RAPIDS MANUFACTURING AND POWER COMPANY.
speechtext:
This matter came before me by reason of an application that the company made to have their plans approved of. It appeared that some time ago, before I became minister, there had been a partial approval of the undertaking, and the parties were of opinion that before they could actually expropriate land they would require, under the statutes, approval of the plan of their works. In view of the fact that we have an International Waterways Commission to whom all questions relating to waters which are wholly or for a part of

their course boundary waters between the United States and Canada, are usually referred, I thought it would be well to refer the matter to that commission. The matter was accordingly referred. If it had not been that I took that view, I think I should have felt it my duty, upon the report which I had from the engineers of my department, to approve of the plans, and the company could have proceeded to expropriate the property. Under these circumstances, I scarcely think it would be right to refuse to the company the extension of time. It may be, the time asked for is too long. It does seem to me that it is unreasonably long; but I think they might fairly be given a reasonable extension. I was informed, and I have no doubt it is the case, that the company already owns a very considerable part of the land rights necessary for the development of the water-power at the place where they propose to develop it, but that they desire to exercise their rights of expropriation in regard to additional property. Parliament having granted them the power by their Act of Incorporation, and there having been delay because of the reference by me to the International Waterways Commission, and and as their time expires early in the coming summer, so that it would have been difficult for them to exercise their powers of expropriation in the meantime, it does seem to me rather reasonable that an extension should be given.

subtopic: CEDAR RAPIDS MANUFACTURING AND POWER COMPANY.
speechtext: Have they shown any evidence of ability to build the works necessary for this power? It is very easy for people to get plans,-it costs very little to do that, and then endeavour to get somebody to buy the rights they have.

subtopic: CEDAR RAPIDS MANUFACTURING AND POWER COMPANY.
speechtext: The people who are interested in the property that is to be developed, and whose names I do not now recall, but who are very respectable people, gave me very positive assurances that they were ready to go ahead and were most anxious to have their plans approved, but I thought it was only courteous to the government of the United States that the plans should be submitted to the Waterways Commission. If I had not taken that ground I do not imagine that they would have been here asking for an extension of time. It seems to me though that the time asked for is longer than they need. If it were shortened by two years I should think it would be ample.

subtopic: CEDAR RAPIDS MANUFACTURING AND POWER COMPANY.
speechtext: Does not the minister think it is time we stopped granting these charters giving rights to water-powers when we know that every day these water-powers are growing in value? They are one of the great assets of this country. The question came up not long ago in the House with reference to a western charter. Before long we will use these water-powers in place of coal, or at any rate, for heating purposes. Is it not time that we stopped granting these charters to private individuals which give them the practical ownership of large water-powers which at the present time are no doubt largely vested in the Dominion? The persons to whom we give these powers very likely do not propose to develop them at all, but they have sense enough to see that before long they will become of great value.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: CEDAR RAPIDS MANUFACTURING AND POWER COMPANY.
speechtext: The company have already acquired, without expropriation, nearly all the land necessary and the only portions that are outstanding of the land required are portions which are owned by non-residents. These non-residents are holding out for an excessive price for the lands which are proposed to be purchased. It will be seen, therefore, that the company have done something to cary out the objects for which they are incorporated.

subtopic: CEDAR RAPIDS MANUFACTURING AND POWER COMPANY.
speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. member who has this Bill in charge whether he knows that himself?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: CEDAR RAPIDS MANUFACTURING AND POWER COMPANY.
speechtext: I only know that it was stated before the committee and I have a letter from the person who is acting as the advocate of the company in which he says that that is really the state of affairs at the present time. Of course, I could not say it from my own knowledge.

subtopic: CEDAR RAPIDS MANUFACTURING AND POWER COMPANY.
speechtext: I do not think that what my hon. friend from Argenteuil (Mr. Per-ley) is contending against is so much the right to expropriate lands as the right to hold these waterways for a period of five years. In view of the fact that the government has taken steps at this session to preserve our natural resources, and has added to the standing committees of the House three committees having that object in view, I think it would not be a bad idea to submit this Bill to the committee on waterways and forestry to say whether, in their opinion, it is wise to allow a company to blanket a water-power for five years.

subtopic: CEDAR RAPIDS MANUFACTURING AND POWER COMPANY.
speechtext:
It seems to me that it would be scarcely fair to this company to do that. Parliament has already given it this charter and has clothed it with the power of developing this water-power and acquiring lands. In pursuance of that authority they have gone ahead, and they have, as I was informed, acquired practically all the land which is necessary for

the development of these powers. We ought to treat this company just as we treat other companies. We scarcely ever refuse to give a reasonable extension of time, parliament having once granted the charter. With regard to the question raised by my hon. friend from Argenteuil (Mr. Perley), I think it is one of a great deal of importance. I think it is a question that is worthy of a good deal of consideration as to whether steps should not be taken for the public control of the various water-powers, particularly the valuable water-powers of the country, but before we should refuse to private individuals the opportunity of developing these powers and rendering them available to industrial purposes which, of course, is a matter of very great public advantage, the government ought to be prepared to undertake the responsibility of their development. My hon. friend will see that if we were to refuse to private companies the authority to develop power without the government being prepared to move forward the result would be to prevent any development at all. We have granted a great many charters to private companies and it seems to me it would not he reasonable to stay our hand just at the present time whatever may be decided upon in future. Having once granted a charter to this company it seems to me that it would be only reasonable that parliament should grant an extension. But I would suggest to the promoter of the Bill, if he is present, that the time be made 1912 instead of 1914. I think that would be ample time to enable this company to exercise all the powers which they might reasonably exercise under the charter in so far as the expropriation of land is concerned.

subtopic: CEDAR RAPIDS MANUFACTURING AND POWER COMPANY.
speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. gentleman who is in charge of this Bill whether there was any opposition to it in the committee?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: CEDAR RAPIDS MANUFACTURING AND POWER COMPANY.
speechtext: An hon. gentleman who was present tells me there was no opposition at all.

subtopic: CEDAR RAPIDS MANUFACTURING AND POWER COMPANY.
speechtext:
The minister says that they got this power from parliament and that they should not now be refused an extension of it. They got their charter but they allowed it to lapse. They acquired it when there was very little attention directed to the water-powers of the country, but since then, the necessity has become more apparent of having some supervision over these very valuable assets belonging to the provinces, in most cases, although, I presume, in this case, this being on the St. Lawrence river, it would probably come under federal authority. But, I think that the provinces should have control over these water-powers. It seems to me that these properties belong to the provinces; therefore, I should think the provinces Mr. PUGSLEY.
would have the right if they saw fit to lease them. I do not believe they should be given away for nothing. It is a mistake and is not good business. They should be leased so that they would yield a very considerable revenue, as time went on, to the province. The province of Ontario, at least, is considering the question of how far to go in taking charge of the water-powers which belong to the province and this, together with the interest which has developed lately in the federal parliament in regard to the question, as well as the public attention which has been directed to it, should cause us to be much more cautious now in dealing with the question than we have been hitherto. Since this charter has run out and they have done nothing, I do not think it would be any very great hardship if we allowed it to die and allowed the property to revert to the province or to the Dominion as the case may be.

subtopic: CEDAR RAPIDS MANUFACTURING AND POWER COMPANY.
speechtext: My hon. friend is in error as to the charter running out. If it had run out there might be some force in what he has said, but the charter has not run out. They came here some time ago asking for the approval of their plans, and they had still quite a number of months within which to exercise the rights contained in the charter. The charter will not expire until some time in June next.

subtopic: CEDAR RAPIDS MANUFACTURING AND POWER COMPANY.
speechtext: This is the last session and it is practically an expiration of the charter.

subtopic: CEDAR RAPIDS MANUFACTURING AND POWER COMPANY.
speechtext: If I had approved of the plan when they came to me, they would have had ample time to expropriate the land before the charter expired. But I thought it proper, as a courtesy to the government of the United States, to refer the whole matter to the International Waterways Commission. What they feel is that there will not be a report from the commission in time to enable them to expropriate the land before the charter expires, and that is why they come here. But I think the extension they ask for is too long, I think it should be made not longer than 1911 or 1912.

subtopic: CEDAR RAPIDS MANUFACTURING AND POWER COMPANY.
speechtext: The minister seems to have only one anxiety, that is, to give them a renewal so that they may expropriate the land. What strikes me is that we are giving them forever, practically, control over the water-power, and if we did not renew the charter at this session of parliament it would die. Since they have kept, practically, the whole limit of the time without taking advantage of it, except doing some preliminary work, I do not think it would be any great hardship, in view of the fact that we are on the eve of starting a new policy with regard to these waterways, if we kept the waterway in the hands of the authorities that own it.

subtopic: CEDAR RAPIDS MANUFACTURING AND POWER COMPANY.
speechtext:
I raised this question merely on general principles. I have nothing to say against this particular project,
I do not know who the gentlemen are that are interested in it. But I agree with what the minister has said. We want to get our powers developed as fast as we can; if the government do not do it, we must find some private corporations to do it. But we ought to consider carefully whether, in the future, we ought not to insist that before we grant any such charters, some evidence of good faith should be given, and some evidence of the ability of the parties to put the work through. We ought to take the stand that no charters of this kind should be granted giving valuable water-powers, when the promoters wish to get them simply for the purposes of speculation, because we all know that these water-powers are going to be of immense value. However, in this case there seems to be no opposition to the Bill in committee, and I think we might agree with the minister's suggestion that the date to which the expropriation powers are extended should be changed from 1914 to 1911. That would give them ample time. If they really mean business, two years are lots of time for them to do all they want to do.

subtopic: CEDAR RAPIDS MANUFACTURING AND POWER COMPANY.
speechtext: I move in amendment, in section 1, line 4, to strike out the word * 1914 ' and substitute therefore the word ' 1911.'

subtopic: THE KOOTENAY AND ARROWHEAD RAILWAY COMPANY.

speechtext: House in committee on Bill (No. 80) respecting the Kootenay and Arrowhead Railway Company.-Mr. George Taylor.

subtopic: THE KOOTENAY AND ARROWHEAD RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: On section 1.

subtopic: THE KOOTENAY AND ARROWHEAD RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I propose to move the amendment of which I have given notice:
The Kbotenay and Arrowhead Railway Company shall within two years after the passing of this Act construct fifteen per cent of the mileage of the unconstructed portion of the railways which it was authorized by section 7, of chapter 70, of the statutes of 1901, to construct and shall complete said railways and put them in operation within five years, and if the said fifteen per cent of mileage is not so constructed, and if the said railways are not so completed and put in operation within the said periods respectively, the powers of construction conferred upon the said company by parliament shall cease Mr. GRAHAM.
and be null and void as respects so much of the said railways as then remains uncompleted.
The day on which this Bill was considered before the Railway Committee there was at the same hour a meeting of the Banking and Commerce Committee which was dealing with the Insurance Bill, and a meeting of the Standing Orders Committee which was dealing with the Canada Life Bill, and as a large number of the members were present at these other important committees there were few at the Railway Committee and my amendment was defeated by the very narrow majority of only two votes. Hence I consider I am amply justified in asking the House to now reconsider this Bill. Then again, by an amendment passed in the Railway Committee they were granted five years to build the railway from Lardo via Duncan up to Arrowhead, which is really the uncompleted portion of the original charter, and by that amendment they say to the House that they are commencing to construct a short line of railway which will be a connecting link between two portions of the railway already connected. There is the further reason in support of my amendment that in 1906 they obtained from parliament an extension of three years for the construction of this portion of the railway, and in that three years they have done absolutely nothing. There is the further reason, that m addition to the privilege of bonding the road for $25,000 a mile there was granted a large cash subsidy per mile which has been paid over to them for that portion of the railway which has already been built. There is a still more important reason and it is that when this charter was first asked for in 1901, there was an influx of prospectors and capitalists into that district in the Kootenay country in anticipation of the road being immediately constructed. This is a very mountainous district having a large number of very beautiful lakes, and minerals being discovered there the prospectors felt that the word of a great corporation like the Canadian Pacific Railway could be relied upon, and so they brought in a large amount of machinery at great cost to develop these mines, only to find that they had been deceived and that the railway would not be built. In addition to that a large number of agricultural settlers have gone into that district on the same understanding and these men have been there for nine years deprived of the fruits of their capital and their labour. I would call the attention of the House further to the fact that there appears in the daily press an article in large type, said to be authorized from headquarters, stating that the company were about to rush this railroad to completion, and with the permission of the committee I shall read that article:

We have news from a reliable source that one of the objects of the Canadian Pacific Railway in stopping work on the Kootenay Central is to rush the construction of the Arrowhead and Kootenay Railway, connecting Revelstoke with the Crow's Nest road, and making Revelstoke the most important railway junction in the province of British Columbia. It is stated the Canadian Pacific Railway now recognize this road must be built without delay if the road is to be in a position to handle the big grain business which is now being developed between the western prairies and the Pacific coast.
There is something very sinister in this article with reference to the reason why the Canadian Pacific Railway did not build the Kootenay Central. Let me say that just a few weeks ago we had before the Railway Committee a Bill applying for an extension of time for the completion of the Kootenay Central Railway and I objected to the extension being granted without a provision being inserted that the road should be commenced within a certain time. Would you believe it, sir, that at that time the Canadian Pacific Railway actually put men to work and announced in the press of the district that they were about to rush the Kootenay road to completion, but just as soon as the Bill passed the House without any provision of the kind I wanted there was a telegram sent out there and the men who were working on the road were withdrawn. In this very same press which announced that the Kootenay Central Railroad would be constructed, we find the statement now made that the reason for the withdrawal of theses men was that th Canadian Pacific Railway Company were about to construct the Arrowhead and Kootenay railroad. We are peculiarly situated in this part of British Columbia in that the railroads have to follow the easiest lines to get through the great mountain ranges and make connection with the outside world, and although these pieces of road are short in themselves it is necessary that they should be constructed in order to develop that part of the province. The amendment which I offer is a fair and reasonable one, inasmuch as it simply asks that they shall construct only 15 per cent of the total mileage covered by this charter, and no doubt some of the members of the committee will be surprised to learn that 15 per cent amounts to only six or seven miles. That does not seem much of an enterprise for a great corporation like the Canadian Pacific Railway to undertake in view of the fact that in their notices in the daily papers and in this very Bill itself they say they will commence the construction of this railroad within two years, and complete and put it in operation within five years. When the Bill was before the Railway Committee the Minister of Railways very justly told us that he had
received resolutions from boards of trade urging him to make provision that the company should construct this line immediately. There has been discussion in the Railway Committee over the formation of some definite scheme to compel companies applying for charters to demonstrate their bona fides by constructing within a reasonable time the railways covered by the charters they ask for, and to my mind there is no simpler way of meeting the difficulty than to provide that a small percentage of the total mileage shall be constructed within a specified time. Surely there can be no hardship in the amendment I offer when it allows this company two years to construct 15 per cent of a road which they themselves declare they will have completed and running in five years. My amendment should appeal to the sense of fairness and justness of every man in this committee. It is not very much of a penalty, indeed it is no penalty at all to ask this company to show their bona fides by constructing within two years 15 per cent of the mileage included in the charter. If I had a map I could show the committee that this line runs from Lardo to Arrowhead. The Arrowhead branch has already been constructed under another charter and runs from the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway to Revelstoke to a point on the Arrow lakes, a portion of the Columbia river. By completing this small link of 40 miles they will have a line giving access to that rich tract of country, opening up mines and agricultural lands. The settlers who have gone in there and the capitalists who have invested money there will be enabled to reap some reward for their labour and investment. I appeal to the committee for support of this amendment as a business proposition.

speakeroldname: Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext: There has never been a scale at this point. Hon. gentlemen have seen some discussions on weights of lumber and it was decided to install this scale.

Does the minister think it proper to charge a scale of this kind to capital account on a road that has been running for 50 years? It seems extraordinary that you cannot get a new chair for an office on the Intercolonial Railway without charging it to capital account. This practice I think is contrary to the rule upon railways and should be stopped.
Absolutely the same thing is done on other railways, it is an addition, it is not even a renewal.

You might charge to capital account a new handle on a door. It is one of the ordinary articles required on a railway. No company ever thinks of charging any of these things to capital. It is a monstrous thing, and would not be thought of in any institution except one that is trying to produce a political effect by showing a surplus.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The amount involved does not affect the principle. The question is not whether the amount is large or small but whether an amount of this kind is a proper charge to capital. If it is a betterment of the road, it is a legitimate capital charge.

The principle is well understood, that every institution of this kind should endeavour, as far as possible, to close its capital account. The principle is not, as the hon. minister seems to think, to charge every new thing to capital. When a railway is fairly on its feet, fairly in Mr. GOODEVE.
operation-I wont say after it has been running for fifty years, but after it has been running for ten years-it is never thought right to charge every little thing of this kind-a $2,500 scale-to capital. There would be no end of it. On that principle, if you put a new wheelbarrow on the platform at a station, you would charge the amount to capital.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And that would be perfectly right. If you have an addition to the stock of the railway, anything that adds to the permanent value of the property it is a proper charge to capital. From the hon. member's (Mr. Barker) large knowledge of railway affairs, I am sure that he will see, on consideration, that this is a matter of principle, not a matter of amount, and that his contention is not well founded.

I have given the thing consideration, and I speak of my own knowledge when I say that large concerns of this kind that are fairly in operation, going concerns, when they want some little thing for the service-a few more trucks around the station or anything of that kind costing a few thousand dollars-never think of charging the amount to capital. What would be the result if they did ? Take a concern like the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway or the Canadian Pacific Railway, which, perhaps, has no capital account; they could not provide these things that are necessary. These concerns spend thousands and thousands in this way, and the" amounts are charged up to maintenance or revenue. It is not necessarily maintenance in a going concern, such expenditures are a proper charge to revenue. I venture to say I can produce to this committee-not at the moment, of course-quotations from authorities on railway operations to establish what I say.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the hon. member will look at the Intercolonial accounts, he will find many expenditures of a similar character charged to capital. And, if they be betterments, I do not think the point admits of any doubt. Sometimes there may be a question as to whether the amount represents a betterment or not. Where a renewal is charged to capital, of course, that is open to criticism. But, if you add a mile to your road, a new station, or anything that will make the property more valuable than before, that is, I submit, a legitimate charge to capital. Of course, no company would want to open a capital account for these trifling things, but if it had an open capital account, these items would be properly chargeable to it.

That is just the point. An ordinary railway has no open capital account, and no company should have an open capital account that has used its capital in establishing a railway system; it

should_ make the business bear itself and carry itself along. Of course, if they are going to add a new branch, that is a different thing, but to say that every petty appliance, or every petty accommodation aiong fifteen hundred miles of railway makes it necessary to keep an open capital account is wholly unreasonable; it would never be thought of. If a company were converting their whole bridge system from wood to steel, or replacing a sixty pound rail with an eighty pound rail, they would charge the difference to capital. But hon. gentlemen opposite a few years ago, charged the whole eighty pounds to capital.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
Yes, they charged the whole eighty pounds to capital, and credited the concern with the scrap rails.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is not what the
hon. member said a moment ago.
They threw the old rails in the scrap and credited them. That is not the principle on which the accounts should be run.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot see the difference, as a matter of principle, between an additional rail to the road and an additional scale to the road. The mere fact that the amount is small does not alter the principle. As I have said no company would open an account for these small amounts, but, when there is an open account, you must choose whether you will charge the amount to one account or to the other. In this case, which account should be chosen? Surely, capital account, for this is clearly a betterment. But the hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker) says there should be no open capital account. Well, we have to differ from him on that point. The hon. gentleman asks what would a railway company do in this case? The Canadian Pacific Railway, for instance, have regularly charged to capital items that the hon. gentleman says, ^n the case of the Intercolonial, should not be charged to capital.

I do not think the hon. minister can find a single instance of that kind. Say, after. ten years, the Canadian Pacific Railway comes here to get authority to issue new capital, does the hon. gentleman suppose that, in the meantime, they have not been buying trucks and other things necessary.for the road?
And they are adding to capital account every year.

When an extremely large expenditure is to be made, one that would put the companies into difficulties, it will be made with a capital expenditure. But this is like a manufacturing establishment putting in a glass window in its office and charging it to capital.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If it was an original
window, it certainly should be charged to capital. Or, even if there was a window, and the company improved its property by putting in a plate-glass front, it ought to charge it to capital.
No manufacturing company in the country would think of keeping open a capital account for such charges- taking down an old front door and putting in a new one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a renewal.

In precisely the same way, an old railway company takes it for granted that, in the carrying on of its business, there are many articles that are to be added new and that they will buy, but they never think of keeping such things in a capital account. And the sooner this railway gets down to that principle, the sooner we shall be able to compare earnings or losses upon this road with the earnings or losses on privately-owned railways.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) does not see the difference between adding a rail or a scale. The road cannot run without rails, but it can run without scales.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, it must weigh its freight.

It can use the scales it already has in other places. It may be a convenience for the traffic at this particular place to have a new scale, but the work was done without it before. A scale I would not regard as a betterment of the road at all, but merely an improvement for the handling of freight. The additions to the roadbed, stations, and so on, I take it would be betterments of the road, but I do not think that an added scale here or there should be regarded as a betterment of the road.
