The final estimate has not come in, but it is about $71,000, perhaps a few dollars under that.
What is the original estimate of the cost of this wharf?
Our own engineer estimated it at $75,000. The work is now finished.

Is the department aware that the concrete work of this wharf has cracked during the last five or six months, and that the wharf is practically useless for any purpose at the present time, and was useless during navigation last fall.
Some little time ago the crack my hon. friend refers to was caused by a vessel striking the pier. It is not at all serious.
Is the department aware that this wharf is not fit to be used in its present condition, and was not last fall.
That is not the report we have from our engineers. The chief engineer himself visited the wharf last-summer, and says it is in good shape.

I am speaking of the crack and the condition the wharf was in at the close of navigation. When the wharf was said to be finished, it was left very much unfinished. The top of the wharf is not finished, it will require two feet of clay or earth to make it fit for teams. The crack was here last fall, and the wharf was practically useless for shipping purposes at the close of navigation, and for some time previous.

Putting a little earth on top is not part of the contract at all. It is a matter of opinion as to the wharf not being useful, my hon. friend is the first who has raised that. Of course, he understands that it is not part of the contract.
If there is something that is not in the contract, 'we want to know what the completed wharf will cost.
The wharf has been used, it is a question perhaps of putting some gravel on it, or something of that kind.
Is it the intention of the department to leave the wharf in the condition it was in last fall?

We will ask our engineer to give us a report after seeing what my hon. friend says, and if there is anything else to be done, we will do it.
Montague branch-land claims, $6,851.51.

This claim and the Murray Harbour branch land claim, and the Vernon River branch land claim, are Exchequer Court judgments. This Montague branch is a small branch six miles long which was opened in 1906. There were certain land claims taken to the Exchequer Court.
How long have these judgments been standing against the government?

Since April and May of last year.
Lachine canal-further amount required to rebuild slope walls, $78,000.

This matter was thoroughly gone into on our main estimates for the canal, and there is in the main estimates already passed an amount to finish this work. That contract was let some years ago for rebuilding these slope walls with concrete, making them practically new walls. After the Cornwall accident last summer our engineer made a thorough examination of these walls, and I asked him to rush the work, because I became alarmed that there might be some other accidents to our canals.
Rideau canal-improvements, $16,000.

Those who were here the other evening probably will remember my explanation that I would take $25,000 out of the main estimates and make the amount in the main estimates $15,000, explaining to the committee that I would put $25,000 in these supplementary estimates because 1 could use it this year, we having advanced that much with this work.
Railways and canals-income-miscellaneous -to provide for expenses preparing plans for the reconstruction of the Quebec bridge- further amount required, $10,500.
We had $25,000 voted last year. This is intended for the work of the board.
Who are preparing these plans? Have you a staff of experts preparing them?

The Board of Engineers, Messrs. Vautelet, Modjeska and Maurice FitzMaurice, and they employ their own staff. We do not even make a recommendation to their staff. I want to let them accept the full responsibility. They have asked us for $10,500 more than they have expended this year up to date.
Intercolonial Railway expenses - further amount required, $500,000.
This estimate was made some time ago. We have got to a period at which we can reduce that by $150,000.
This is for working expenses?	,	.
Working expenses. There will be a considerable discussion no 'doubt on the main estimates on the item 'for working expenses. This will make the item $350,000.
How did you underestimate so much last year for working expenses? Was that due to the election?

No, that was the estimate they gave me. But we had a supplementary vote last year to make the amount up to $9,000,000. They underestimated the year before about $1,500,000.
Windsor Branch Railway-maintenance- further amount required, $7,000.
We are relaying the Windsor branch with a heavier rail out of revenue account.
What weight of rail are you putting down there?

It has been a 56-pound rail and we are replacing it with 67-pound fails that we have at the present time.
' Mr. BLAIN. Where are the rails manufactured that are put down on the Intercolonial Railway?
They are all manufactured in Canada, either at Sydney or the Soo.
What is the piice now?

Militia and defence-chargeable to income- pay and allowances-further amount required, $170,000.
' Sir FREDERICK BORDEN (Minister of Militia and Defence). This is simply _ a readjustment of the vote. We are not increasing the vote of the current year a single dollar, but some votes were larger than were required and others were smaller. It is proposed to take these votes, amounting altogether to $300,000, and not 'to use certain votes which I will read which were voted for the current year and are not required.
Engineers' services	$ 90,000
Militia stores	 65,000
Dominion arsenal	 60,000
Customs dues	 85,000
Total	$300,000
This vote is required for the permanent force.
What has been done with regard to the money which is now due to the men at Halifax? Has any arrangement been made by which they will get paid Within a short time?
The moment this vote passes the House, I understand from the Minister of Finance, the Auditor General will be ready to issue a cheque.
They will be able to get their money to-morrow if we pass it to-hight?
Yes.

Then I will be very glad to see it passed.
Annual drill - further amount required, $105,000.

I would like to ask the minister if the annual training school for students in the city of Winnipeg has been held at the usual time this spring?
' Sir FREDERICK BORDEN. I am not absolutely certain, but I think it has. At any rate if it has not it will be held now.

I understood when I was 'home that the school had not been held at the usual time, but that it had been post-'poned until April or thereabouts.
' Sir FREDERICK BORDEN. It is possible.

There was a great deal of dissatisfaction among the young men who reside in the country and who will be busy

with their farming operations at that time of the year. They will be debarred from attending the school by reason of the postponement.

I hope that will not be the case, but when this vote has been taken the school will be called at once.
Transport - further amount required, $12,500.
What transport is this- material or persons?

This is the ordinary transport connected with the camps and schools.
Royal military college-further amount required, $12,500.
Why is there more money required for the Military College?

There is not a vacant place in the college and one or two instructors have had to be added.
Post Office Department, $240,000.

This is required to meet the expenditure for rural mail delivery, the opening of new post offices and new postal routes, particularly in the western provinces, and the increased frequency of existing services on existing routes.
How much for each of these services?

Between $80,000 and $85,000 is estimated for rural mail delivery; the balance is for the other purposes. Demands are pouring in every day for the opening of new post offices, particularly in the western provinces, which affords an excellent barometer of the progress of the west.
Is the Postmaster General providing for additional accommodation in the Dartmouth post office where it is so badly needed?

The leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden) called my attention to this matter yesterday and pointed out that the Dartmouth office is quite too small for the business done there. This morning I asked the deputy minister to get a report from our inspector at Halifax and I will try to convince my colleagues that something should be done this year.

I would remind the Postmaster General that there is a request before his department for the opening of a post office at Mount Pleasant in Peel county. I would also ask the hon. gentleman to have his inspector examine into the mail routes in that county. These routes were established a great many years ago; since that time some new railways have

been constructed necessitating a rearrangement of the mail service, to which I think with benefit to the public the other mail routes might be made to conform. The committee will be surprised to know that in some parts of that old county of Peel the people have not yet a daily mail service. It would be in the public interest if the Postmaster General would have his inspector make an adjustment of the mail routes, and while it would not increase the general expenditure much it would be a great convenience to the people.
My hon. friend (Mr. Blain) has already written to me on the subject, and I will certainly ask the inspector to make a report.

In October last there was considerable talk about the erection of a new post office in the village of Lake-field where the postal accommodation is very inadequate, but I fail to see any appropriation in the estimates for that building although the Postmaster General is providing post office buildings in many places with not half the population of Lake-field. I trust that in the near future he will erect a post office there.
The erection of a post office comes under the Department of Public Works, but of course on the recommendation of the postal authorities. I will make a note of the request of my hon. friend.
I wish to direct the attention of the Postmaster General to the mail contract up the Cariboo road in British Columbia.
Is that the old trail?

Yes. In reply to questions which I asked in the House I was informed that the present contractors receive $24,750 per year and that the contract had not been let by tender since 1897. This is probably the most important mail contract in the west.
What is the mileage ?

The mileage with the side routes must be 400 or 500 miles. In 1862 or 1863 the first contract was let going up to Barkerville, about 280 miles north of the main line at Ashcroft. This is the country built up by the great mining rush in 1858 and 1859. From 1862 until 1896, this very important mail contract had always been let by open tender and for periods of four years. Prior to 1896, from Ashcroft to Lillooet, which is a separate line, about 36 miles, was let with the same contract; but as the country got developed, the policy was adopted-I think a wise policy-of letting these 36 miles by four year contracts separately and letting them direct by the government. In 1897 this big

contract of $24,750 was let to an eastern firm and since that time, probably the minister hardly realizes the fact that there have been absolutely no calls for tenders at all, and in addition the branch lines, of which there are quite a number, have not been let separately, as they should have been, by four years contract, but were merged in this main contract. There are four of these branch lines-one from Clinton via Big Bar and Dog Creek to Alkali lake, 112 miles and return; another one from the 150 mile house to Harper's camp; another one from the 150 mile house to Quesnel Forks; another to Alexis creek, Chilcotin. I want to speak of what I regard as an evil, and that is having these side lines merged in the main contract. The past practice has been for the company which has the main contract to sublet these lines by yearly contract. Take No. 4 from the 150 mile house to Alexis creek as an example; this line is 172 miles return trip, and it takes the contractor five days to do it. That contract has been sublet for $1,100. The passengers and express matter are so small that they add very little to the contractor's profits, and we think it rather absurd that a man, only equipped with four horses, should be doing 172 miles round trip in a country such as that Cariboo district. It is practically impossible, under the circumstances, for him to give a satisfactory service. It is bad enough in ordinary times, but An bad roads and bad weather it is impossible. The question may be put, why did this man take the contract at so small a sum ? The answer he gave to this question was that he had learned his lesson and would never do it again. Next year of course, the company will again let out that contract at as small a figure as they can.
What is the starting point of the main contract ?

From Ashcroft. The letting of these side contracts is on an entirely wrong principle. They should not be sublet by the year. The result of this practice is that a number of people will tender who do not realize that they are tendering at absurdly low figures, and they get stuck and lose money, and at the end of the year they throw up the contract. In the meantime the public is badly served and there is profound dissatisfaction through the country. The proper practice would be that which was always pursued prior to 1896, namely, to let each of the side contracts directly by the department for four years after calling for tenders. The contractor has then time to equip himself in good shape for doing the work and will give better satisfaction. I wish now to say a word about the mail contractors. I am not putting it too strongly when I say there 108
is throughout the whole of that country very strong resentment regarding the methods followed. 1 am not saying whether this company is getting too much or too little ; but I would point out that a large and important company of that kind, with ramifications of one kind or another, can exert a very strong political influence, and very naturally will exert it on behalf of this government which gives it this $24,000 per year contract without any call for tenders. The district of Cariboo is really worse off to-day than in former days because this company while having a monopoly, though not perhaps giving a worse service than the people formerly had, is charging higher fares. Formerly return fares were given at reduced rates but there are none such today. If that contract were thrown open to tender, there should be some fixed rate of fares in the public interest because the only possible way the people have of transportation over that 280 miles is by this means.
I remember that when this matter was up before, the minister said that the policy of his department was to let all the contracts by tender, but no public tender has ever been invited for this important work since early in 1897. And a peculiar thing is that it is a Toronto firm which has the contract. What would my hon. friends from Ontario think if there was a contract north of Toronto for a 280 mile mail route to be let and if that contract had been let by tender 12 years ago to a British Columbia firm, and instead of new tenders being invited every four years, that contract were renewed from year to year without tenders and without any opportunity being given any Ontario firm to bid for it? I am sure the minister will see that the Toronto people would, under the circumstances, feel that they had a very strong grievance. The contract was renewed early last summer. I do not know whether it is possible to cancel that contract, but at all events I hope that when the time comes to renew it, the minister will see his way clear to deal with it in that spirit in which he promised to deal with all those matters and throw it open to public competition. I am expressing the opinion, not only of my own friends, but of the minister's all through that country, when I say that he would give profound satisfaction to the people of that part of British Columbia,-a part which is not served by railways-if he would throw open that important contract to public tender and also adopt the policy of letting all those side lines directly by four years' contracts in the same manner.

The hon. gentleman has made what I call a very fair criticism of this contract. In 1897 my predecessor, Sir



William Mulock, advertised for tenders and this company, the British Columbia Express Company, which is a Toronto firm, were the lowest tenderers and the department awarded the contract to them. This is a peculiar section of the country and the contractors have to make quite an outlay in order to cover that immense territory It is a very difficult country to travel over. The contract has been renewed twice since 1897, because this is a four year contract. The last time it was renewed, I think on representations made to the postal authorities at Ottawa-for I do not know enough of the country to decide such a contract myself-that if we advertised for tenders we would receive tenders but not from any one who would be in a position to cover that immense territory as well as the present contractors do it. I must say that we have not received any complaint as to the manner in which the contract is carried out. Tlie government decided to renew the contract with this firm. However the hon. gentleman (Mr. Burrell) comes from that section of the country and the grievance which he ventilates is in reference not to the main contract but to the side lines which are sublet by the British Columbia Express Company. His representations have been noted and I will see that the company carries out the contract, not only according to the letter but in the spirit in which it was given. I think my hon. friend will agree that this company gives a very good service. The proper way, I know, is to call for tenders, the law is clear on that; but the law also says that when a contract has been faithfully carried out the Postmaster General is at liberty to renew it at the same figure. I cannot increase the amount involved in a contrcat, but I can renew a contract at the same figure, provided the public interest is safeguarded. I can give a similar instance in the Yukon. We have two large contracts there, one with the railway company. Of course we have always renewed the contract with the railway company, and we are practically at their mercy. They are equipped with mail cars and are in a position to carry the mails over their railway to the best advantage; but the mail has to be carried part way to Dawson city by the lakes and the river. We have tried to cut the contract in two, calling for tenders for the lake and river section and allowing the railway the usual mileage allowance, but we cannot succeed because the railway company is the only one sufficiently equipped for the carrying out of the balance of the contract; so, although the amount is large, it has to be paid, and we make no profit out of that district. That is to say, the expenditure exceeds the revenue, but, of course, we have to give postal facilities to the Yukon Territory. ^ There is another somewhat similar case in the Yukon. If it is true that the Mr. LEMIEUX.
British Columbia Express Company farms out the side service at a much lower rate than the one paid to the company by the department, then undoubtedly there is room for improvement.
I hope the minister does not think I am impugning his bona fides in the matter?
On the whole the hon gentleman admits the service is good.

If his line of argument was good in this present case, it was equally gcod in 1896, when other men had the contract, for not changing then, but the department then took the ground that it would be advisable in the interests of the country to throw this contract open to tender. , They then threw down a company with a large equipment.
Was not the route changed and extended?

The former company had only the main contract, but the department included the branch lines instead of letting them separately. I think there is no doubt there would be bona fide tenders if the minister called for them from men who would be able to carry on that work. It might happen that they would find it necessary to purchase a large portion of the present contractor's outfit, as happened when the contract was changed before; but I am positive it would be in the interests of the country and of the government to pursue the usual method of throwing the whole matter open to tender.
I would call attention to another small contract from Lytton up to Lillooet, a distance of 40 miles, which was also renewed without tender. I knew, of course, that the minister was not familiar with the country.
I am familiar with every foot of it and appreciate the sentiment of the people there, and I have no axe to grind, political or otherwise. I simply desire to satisfy the general feeling_ of that whole country, and I assure the minister that his general policy is just as applicable to that country as to any other part of the Dominion.

I may be a little out of order and a little late in the appeal that I desire to make to the Postmaster General, but I was not present when the main estimates were up and possibly I may be allowed to speak now. I desire to make an appeal on behalf of the letter carriers of the city of St. Thomas. I have been observing the Postmaster General for a couple of months, and am inclined to think that he is disposed to be fair, and kind, and even generous. In fact, I had formed that opinion of the Postmaster General before I had the pleasure of seeing him, because he was kind enough to appoint these letter carriers in the city of St. Thomas just two or three

weeks before the elections, and they assisted me materially in distributing campaign literature. They all voted against me, but they are good fellows and they are doing good work and working long hours.
I am sincere about this. These men are living in the city of St. Thomas, where the cost of living is about as high as in Ottawa. I do not think there is another place of its size in Ontario where the cost of living is as high as it is in St. Thomas. There are reasons for that which I could mention. These letter carriers are receiving $1.50 per day. Now, does the Postmaster General think that a man with a wife and family can live, and live decently m a city like St. Thomas, on $1.50 a day ?
I believe that the servants in the Postmaster General's Department, are the only class of public servants of Canada who, as a class, are under paid. The people of this country ought to be ashamed of themselves to take the services of postmasters and letter carriers for the paltry pittances they pay them. I know the case of one man who travels twenty miles a day each way-forty miles a day-carrying the mail, and he gets $230.
By tender ?

Possibly. I have heard
a good deal about tenders since I have had the honour of a seat in this House. In many cases, the answer seems to be regarded as complete when it is to the effect that tenders were advertised for and the lowest tender was accepted. I do not know that that is a conclusive argument in a great many cases. I think the officers of one of these public departments ought to be in a position to instruct the head of the department what is a fair price to pay for the fair services they render, and, if the tender is very much more than a fair price, the department ought to Tefuse to accept it. On the other hand, in these other matters, I do not believe in the people of this country taking the services of public servants for a great deal less than they are actually worth. If the Postmaster General will excuse me for repeating. I would appeal to him as a man on behalf of these men-not political friends of mine, but decent men, putting in long hours and not adequately paid. Men breaking stone on the street get more than do these people who are working long hours delivering mail matter to the people of St. Thomas.

There is an old English dictum ' Fine words butter no parsnips.' I intend to act, not say much about the letter carriers. I will ask the hon. member to wait until next week, when something will probably be done for the letter carriers.

I desire to speak also with reference to the postmasters. I have been looking into the matter, and I find
that in East Elgin there are eight post offices, the keepers of which receive eleven cents a day, and no rent allowance. That is too bad. These offices are open from eight to ten hours a day. I am pleased to say that the Postmaster General has changed the mail routes so that people are able to get the daily papers. There are nine places in which the rent allowance is $6 a year. But I draw particular attention to these eight places where the postmasters receive eleven cents a day and no rent allowance. The hon. minister the Postmaster General has a surplus. I know what he will say-that the revenues from these post offices do not warrant raising the salary. But I do not see how they can afford to keep the places open for the length of time they do and give the public good service, unless their salaries are increased. I have no political object in advocating this, these people are not supporters of mine, but they speak to me about this frequently. I have mentioned the matter to the minister privately, but I feel it my duty to take advantage of the discussion on this item to bring the matter before the minister in this way. I do not know whether he will feel like making a promise to raise the salaries, particularly of those who get no rent allowance. I would like to hear from him on the subject.

I could not give an answer at once; I should need to look into each case. If the hon. member will send me the names, I will investigate. Sometimes it happens that, in our 14,000 offices a mistake may be made as regards the rental and fuel allowance. And, as my hon. friend (Mr. Marshall) knows, the salary allowances are based on the revenue of each office. So, it varies. Some years, an office will receive the allowance, but if, next year, it is below a certain figure, it is deprived of the allowance. We must have a rule that applies automatically to every office. But, as I have said, mistakes are sometimes made. If the hon. member will send me the names, I will look into the matter.

I would like to make a similar plea on behalf of the postmasters and mail carriers of New Westminster. I would ask the Minister of Labour (Mr. Lemieux) whether it is not possible for him to use his influence with his colleague the Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) to have the fair wage clause, of which we hear a good deal in connection with the Department of Labour, applied to the transactions of the Post Office Department, so that the department might have the experience that private employers all over the country have when they are working on contracts for the government. It is quite proper that private employers should have the experience to which they

are treated by the Minister of Labour. When the government lets a contract to a . private employer, it puts him in a situation that the employees shall be paid a fair wage, which is stated so that there may be no mistake. I would suggest that the Minister of Labour have the Postmaster General do something of the same kind, and, that when contracts are awarded, particularly for the carriage of the mails, he should not ask that it be done at the lowest price, but fix the rate, so that the mail carriers may be paid a fair price for their services, which we can well afford to pay for. I am quite aware that the Postmaster General is one of the most progressive of ministers, and that he has made many improvements in his department. I do not want to appear as crowding him too much, but I think it would be a good idea to act on the lines suggested and to increase the pay of this staff.

I will bring the Postmaster General and the Minister of Labour together, and if they do not agree, I will take them before a conciliation board.
Further amount required (including compensation to the following railway mail clerks for medical and other expenses and loss of personal effects: E. A. Hartling, $118.50; C. E. O'Reilly, $468; W. W. Frost, $20; J H. Kelly, $76, and A. Chabot, $20, $80,000.

This amount is to complete payment for the current year, $1,000; travelling charges and expenses of inspectors and other officials, $39,297; stationery, printing, advertisements, special postage stamps, $10,000; various items of miscellaneous expenditure, such as letter carriers' uniforms, wages of labourers, charwomen, telephone and telegraph messengers, $20,000. The balance is to pay certain of our mail clerks who have been injured during their service on board trains. Mr. Hartling was employed as a railway mail clerk since September, 1895, and in an accident on the Intercolonial in April 1903, and again in 1907, he lost his clothing and other personal effects. Mr. O'Reilly also met with an accident on the Intercolonial on the 26th of February, and he asks for this amount to pay medical and other attendance, lost clothing, and mileage allowance. Mr. Frost was employed as a railway mail clerk, and met with an accident on the Intercolonial, as did also Mr. Kelly and Mr. Chabot. These various items make up the amount of $80,000. The accounts have all been verified by the Auditor General. The committee will notice that some of these accidents took place some years ago, but we did not know whether the amount should be paid by the Post Office Department or by the Railway Department. We Mr. J. D. TATLOR
had to get the opinion of the Minister of Justice, who decides that they should be paid by the Post Office Department.

This item furnishes another argument in favour 'of increasing the salaries of railway mail clerks. These men are subject to railway accidents more than the ordinary citizen, because they are nearly all the time on railway trains. I have received a, circular and letters from mail clerks asking for the consideration of the department. They have to make very long runs, and suffer many hardships, as well as being exposed to danger. I would ask the minister, when he is dealing with other employees in his department, if he will kindly consider the railway mail clerks.
I received a delegation the other day, and I have a memorandum of the _ Railway Mail Clerks' Association, which is being considered.
Is the minister able to form any estimate of the profits from the special issue of stamps?
I would not venture to give a figure. If the hon. gentleman will put a question on the Order Paper, I will procure the information.

Last session when these estimates were up, the Postmaster General said a few words with regard to the possibility of providing a special stamp to be used at Christmas time for the benefit of the movement against tuberculosis. At that time, when I asked him a question, I thought the Postmaster General gave an answer which was fairly favourable, and that he was really thinking of doing something of the kind last Christmas; but as he did not do so, I suppose he must have changed his mind.

I have not changed my mind on the subject. I think I informed my hon. friend privately last year when the question came up, that the reason why I thought it unadvisable to issue a special stamp for the benefit of the tuberculosis hospital, was that we had just issued a series of stamps in connection with the Quebec Tercentenary. Besides, it is not considered advisable for any country to multiply special stamps; in fact, it is considered infra dignitatem by the Postal Union to issue special stamps unless it is for such purposes as that of last summer. But I can assure my hon. friend, and all the friends of the hospital fund, and of the movement against tuberculosis, that it is my desire and my aim to help as much as possible that' deserving movement. If it is clearly demonstrated that the issuing of such a special stamp, as is issued in Denmark, and I believe in one or two

other countries in Europe, would yield an amount which will substantially aid that fund, then I am open to conviction. In fact I have been reading many papers on the subject, and I hope that the time may come when I shall be able to realize the hon. gentleman's wishes.
I would call the attention of the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller) to these remarks of the Postmaster General. I hope he has been listening to them.

I have received a petition from the railway mail clerks, and while I do not desire to take up the time of the committee at this stage, I find another feature is presented by the correspondence susequently received, and that is in respect to a class of clerks who have not passed the examination and are not on the regular staff, but are nevertheless performing the services of those officials. It appears they are receiving very meagre remuneration, although they are obliged to travel long distances, and are subject to the same chances of accident as the others. They respectfully request that the minister will consider their petition for an increase of salary when he deals with the permanent clerks.
Further amount required for miscellaneous expenditure, 1908-9, Department of Labour, including printing and stationery, allowance to correspondents, travelling expenses, &c., $6,500.

This amount is required to meet the estimated expenditures to the end of the financial year. The expenditure is due to the heavy travelling expenses of the various officers of the department and to the increased charges for printing, &c.
Amount required to provide for the expenses of W. L. Mackenzie King, M.P., as a representative of Canada at the Joint Opium Conference at Shanghai, China, $5,500.

This amount is required to provide for the expenses of Mr. Mackenzie King as the representative of Canada at the joint Opium Conference at Shanghai, China. The committee knows the object of the conference. For some years there has been a desire to suppress the use of opium and morphine in China, and the great powers, especially Great Britain and the United States of America, have decided, with the consent of China, to call a conference in order to study the question as to what are the best means of suppressing that evil. Canada was invited by the foreign office in London to join that conference. Mr. Mackenzie King was especially well equipped to take part in it. He had studied this question of the opium traffic and last year we introduced a Bill into
this House to suppress it in Canada. Mr. Mackenzie King is now in China; he has taken part in the conference, as usual, to his credit and to the credit of the country to which he belongs. I have not yet his report, but from what I have seen of the cables that appeared in the London 'Times' Mr. Mackenzie King has been one of the leading men in the conference.
Who are taking part in the conference?

The conference is between the different nations, Great Britain, the United States, Germany, France, China and Japan, and perhaps others, but I name the large powers which have interests in the far east. The object of the conference is to suppress gradually the use of opium and morphine.
What is the official language ?
The official language is English.
I suppose we shall have details of this expenditure later on?

Yes; Mt. King is accompanied by a secretary.
Civil governnemt-Governor General's secretary's office-contingencies-further amount required, $6,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is an additional sum required for the contingencies of the Governor General's office chiefly due to the increase in the cost of telegrams. There has been a very large amount of cable business.
Office of the Auditor General-contingencies -clerical and other assistance-to pay the following extra clerks from the 28th June, 1909, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act:-C. M. Low, M. A. Reid, D. M. Gibson, W. M. Greenshields, E. M. Stitt, E. M. Fraser, Bertha McCuaig, :M. (Macdonald, Isabella MIntosh, L. Chartrand and H. R. Washington, $500.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Under the Civil Service Act the Auditor General had employed a number of temporary clerks who could only be employed, according to the strict wording of the Act, for four months. When the four months expired, to comply strictly writh the Act, he would be obliged to dismiss these clerks and bring in others. As they were engaged in work that was rather urgent, checking the election officers' accounts, the Auditor General came to me and said that he thought it was undesirable that these officers should go. I agreed with him that he should continue them for a short time, although I pointed out that it would necessitate a special vote as they are not employed in strict accordance with the Civil Service Act.
This is an item in regard to which my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) wished to make some remarks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would suggest that the item pass and an opportunity will be given to the hon. gentleman to discuss it at a future time. I would like to get this through this evening. It is only $500.
My hon. friend from North Toronto mentioned this particularly to me and said that if it came up he would like to have it stand over.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It will delay the Supply Bill. If my hon. friend presses it I cannot insist upon it going through, but I will give my hon. friend the assurance that there will be abundant opportunity for discussing it and I hope he will allow it to pass under these conditions.
Of course we ought to get rid of those words 'notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act.' I thought we had got rid of them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think we have got Tid of them pretty well.
Is there any need of having them there ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is the old form. If my hon. friend thinks it will help to leave them out I will not object.
Who appointed these clerks ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Auditor General.
Appointed by himself ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, I think so. The practice in past years was for the Minister of Finance to appoint them. I was away at the time and I think the Auditor General appointed them himself. I know nothing to the contrary.

There would be every objection, from my point of view, to the government appointing any clerks in the audit
office.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They have always been appointed by the government.
I think that is a mistake. The commission that has been created should appoint the staff in the Auditor General's office.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Civil Service Act makes no distinction between the Auditor General's office and any other office.
It is not intended that these clerks shall continue to be employed beyond a certain period?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, the vote is only $500 for the whole of them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: I thought that possibly that was for the reason that the fiscal year terminates on the 31st of March and you only require to make provision for five weeks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are only there for a short time and only for the special purpose of dealing with the accounts of the election officers.

Assuming that the circumstances are such as the hon. Minister of Finance has disclosed, the case is not as grave as I thought it was. But I think it is extremely desirable that we should not see this memorandum appearing in the estimates. It has been of frequent occurrence in the past although, I am glad to say, it has been of rather infrequent occurrence this session. It seems to me that it should disappear altogether. My attention was directed to this item by my hon. friend from North Toronto who desired to make some inquiries in regard to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not see that the words are very important and they can be stricken out. We have to get authority to pay the money.
Department of Finance and Treasui'y Board-contingencies-funther amount required, $2,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The sum required for the year was under-estimated and we need an additional vote.
Marine and Fisheries Department-amount required to pay salary of Mr. Oswald L. McLeod at the rate of $800 per annum, $363.41.

Mr. McLeod was appointed on the 18th of October, 1898, and owing to his special qualifications in the hardware trade he was to receive a salary of $800, but only $500, the usual salary of a temporary clerk was allowed, the Department of Justice being of the opinion that he should rank as a temporary officer. Considering the nature of Mr. McLeod's work it was thought he should have a salary of $800 and this vote is to give him that salary. It was impossible for him to present himself for competitive examination because no examination was held, but he will do so at the next examination.
To complete voters' lists for general election, 4908, $22,000.
Is this to pay the King's Printer?

Yes.
To provide for promotion of W. A. Lalonde from permanent messengers' staff to third-class clerk at $800, $166.66.
Has this officer a certificate?

He was the personal messenger of the late Speaker, and at the

elose of last session he was placed in charge of the blue book-room.
Did he require to pass an examination?

He was appointed at the end of last session before the Civil Service Act came into force.
To provide increases in the salaries of the following officers and clerks of the House of Commons from April 1, 1908. .T. B. R. La-plante, $700, R. R. Tremblay $200, E. Query $200, E. Naubert $100, $1,200.
Are these increases in accordance with the statute?

These increases were granted by the Board of Internal Economy before the Civil Service Act came into force.
Debates, $25,000.
Last session was the longest session in the history of this parliament and the cost of publishing the debates was greater than usual.
Does this include salaries?

Yes.
Additional amount required for steamship subsidies between Canada and Great Britain, $15,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This subsidy is payable in proportion to the number of passengers and according to the class of vessel, so that it is not a fixed sum, and this additional amount is required to close up the accounts for the year. It is the ordinary Allan and Canadian Pacific Railway subsidy.
Further amount required for the construction of an ice-breaking steamer for the Northumberland straits, $215,000.
We have passed a contract for the construction of this icebreaker for the sum of $500,000, and this amount of $215,000 is to pav the progress estimate due before March 31.
There is an item in the main estimates?
Yes. Next year we will pay the balance of the contract.
We can have any discussion we like on the main estimates?

Yes.
Amount required to pay the pension of the pilot, F. X. Lamarre, from October 1, 1908, to March 31, 1909, at the rate of $300 a year, $150.

This is a sum which has to be paid this pilot for his superannuation.
Lime Kiln crossing-further amount required to pay the outstanding account in connection with the chartering of tug for Lime Kiln crossing, $2,000.
The sum of $10,000 has been put in the estimates to provide for this expenditure. It was expected that the service would expire October 1, but it extended to December 8.
Is that also in the main estimates?

Yes.
Further amount required for the care of sick seamen in marine hospitals and the building and repairs to marine hospitals, $5,000.
Owing to an epidemic of smallpox and scarlet fever, it has been necessary to have added $5,000 to the vote provided for this year.
What building is the hon. gentleman doing?

We are not doing any building. This is a general vote put yearly in the estimates for the care of sick seamen and the building and repairs to marine hospitals. That is the way it is always worded.
Marine biological stations-to provide for unforeseen expenses in connection with the construction of biological stations at St. Andrews, New Brunswick, and Vancouver island, $5,000.
We have built two stations, one at St. Andrews and the other in British Columbia, and this amount is to pay the balance due.
What will be the nature of the work carried on at this station in British Columbia?

These stations are for the purpose of studying the habits of the fish. The expenditure is under the control of scientific men, who are good enough to devote a part of their time to those researches. The board is composed of Prof. Prince, chairman, and a number of other university professors.

There is one line in which a station of this kind could do very useful service. The most important of the fishing industries in British Columbia is that of the sockeye salmon. We have been making large expenditures during a number of years in +be effort to construct enough hatcheries to increase the supply of the sock eye, but notwithstanding all these efforts, and although proper attention has been paid to preserving the sockeye from depredation by fishermen or otherwise, we find that the supply of the salmon is not increasing, but remains about stationary._ The conclusion seems inevitable that there must be some cause for this which has not yet been recognized. There must be some cause, apart from anv suggestion of failure of the hatcheries to secure to us an abundant supply of salmon. So far as we can

see, the hatcheries are doing good work, and if there were no cause operating against them, we should have a yearly increasing supply instead of the supply retrograding or remaining stationary. Would it be part of the purpose of a station of this kind to pursue investigations to ascertain whether there are other fish preying on these salmon in their haunts between the time they leave their hatching grounds on the Fraser river and their return four years later? If we could find out what fish prey on the salmon and devise means of dealing with them, and guard against the efforts of the hatcheries being made nugatory, this station would be worth many times the money proposed to be spent on it.

I am very glad that my hon. friend has brought this to my attention. I shall take care to communicate his observations to the professor in charge. So far as regards the work done, we have obtained very useful information regarding the life and habits of the fish and no doubt the matter my hon. friend has brought to our attention might be properly investigated by the board. I shall bring it to the attention of Professor Prince and the other members of the Board.
To provide for expenses in connection with the International Fisheries Commission, including an amount equivalent to the difference between $2,800 and $4,000, being an increase to be granted to Prof. E. E. Prince since December 1, 1908, $5,400.

This is for the purpose of paying the expenses in connection with the International Fisheries Commission, and also to provide for the salary of Professor Prince. He was formerly paid a salary of $2,800, but in view of the fact that he has been appointed International Commissioner, it was thought advisable to increase his salary to $4,000.
Will the hon. minister state the general scope of this commission?

The commission was appointed in virtue of a treaty signed in the spring of 1908. That treaty provided for the appointment of two commissioners, one by the American government and the other by the Canadian, for the purpose of drafting regulations covering what are called the boundary waters, that is to say, the waters which divide Canada from the United States, waters like the southern part of the Strait of Georgia and the Strait of San Juan de Fuca. Then there are the great lakes of Ontario with their connecting rivers and a part of the St. Lawrence which is boundary water. There are also some lakes in the province of Quebec and in the States of Vermont, New Hampshire and Maine, the River St. John, the River St. Croix and Passamaquoddy bay. The two commissioners were formally Mr. J. D. TAYLOR.
appointed, Mr. Bastedo on behalf of Canada and Dr. Jordan, of Stanford University, California, on behalf of the American government. Mr. Bastedo later accepted a position in the Department of Trade and Commerce and resigned his position on the International Commission. Professor Prince has been appointed to represent Canada. The two commmissioners have held some meetings and Professor Prince is leaving in a few days for the west to meet Professor Jordan. Professor Prince has been instructed to confer while in the west with the provincial authorities of British Columbia.

Why is the whole of the St. John river included in that treaty? Only a small portion of the St. John river forms part of the boundary between the two countries and the greater part of it is far away from the boundary. I have never heard any reason why the whole river should be included in the treaty. The minister knows that Grand Falls creates a perfect block to any sea fish going any further up the river and yet the boundary portion of the St. John river is away above Grand Falls.

The part of the St. John river which is in the state of Maine is, I understand, of great importance to the fisheries, and at the same time some works are being carried on on that river and its tributaries which were detrimental to the interests of the fisheries. It was considered advisable on that account that we should have an opportunity of seeing that proper regulations were made in that part of the river for the purpose of protecting not only our own fisheries, but also the fisheries in that part of the river which is in the state of Maine. Of course if we were going to make regulations with regard to the part of the river in the state of Maine, it was also advisable that the commission should have the same authority on that part of the river which is in Canada. That was why the St. John river was included and the probability is that it is more in the interests of Canadians than of Americans to have that river placed under the control of the commission's regulations.
That is merely with regard to the control of lumber mills and sawdust.

Sawdust particularly. My hon. friend is aware that the sawdust thrown in that part of the St. John river which is in the United States is detrimental to the fisheries, and of course this would give the commissioners an opportunity to deal with that important question, which affects most seriously the interest of our fishermen.

Is it a fact that there can be no regulation now with respect t*

the fisheries of the St. John river without the consent of the commissioner of the United States government and that that would extend even down to the harbour of St. John?

Not necessarily. If the commissioners make no regulations with regard to the part of the river which is in Canada, or make regulations with regard to certain things, such as the size of mesh, it would not prevent our making regulations also with regard to close seasons or otherwise. It will of course give jurisdiction to the two commissioners, if they find it advisable to make regulations.
As I understand, any regulations promulgated by this Interna'-tional Commission become effective without the consent of this parliament.

If I remember rightly the treaty provides that the federal governments of the two countries will have to pass legislation to make the regulations of the commissioners effective. The regulations will have to be submitted to parliament to become effective.
And have the approval of parliament before becoming effective?

I do not know that they would have to receive the approval of parliament. Of course it would come to about the same thing, but I think a clause of the treaty provides that in order to put those regulations in force, parliament will have to enact the necessary laws.

But we cannot have a regulation without the consent of a citizen of a foreign country. Even the regulations prohibiting and fixing the time for fishing in the St. John river must have the consent of a citizen of a foreign country.

Not necessarily, because if the Commissioners do not agree upon the regulations which ought to be put in force, each country will be absolutely free to make the regulations which it considers advisable in the territory which is within its country.
On what points would Professor Prince consult the provincial government of British Columbia?
On the general question of fisheries there, on the nature of the regulations which they would consider best designed to protect our fisheries.
Have they authority in the matter of regulations?

No. The provincial authorities have nothing to do with the drafting of regulations, but the government thought that it would be advisable to have
a conference with the provincial governments before these regulations should be formally drafted. My hon. friend knows that by the British North America Act and by the judgment of the Privy Council of 1898 it was formally decided that the regulation of fisheries was entirely under the control of the federal government; no regulations can be legal except those passed by the federal authorities and as a consequence the provincial authorities have nothing to do with the drafting of regulations. And, as they have some proprietary rights in the fisheries, I thought that, before the regulations were formally adopted, we should have a conference with the provincial authorities. My hon. friend, perhaps, is aware that, some time ago, I had a conference, along with Professor Prince, with the representatives of New Brunswick, Quebec, and Ontario, and discussed the questions which might be raised when these regulations came to be drafted. Our intention was also to call representatives of the British Columbia government, but as British Columbia was far away from the seat of the Dominion government, I thought it would be more advisable that Professor Prince should see the provincial authorities when going to California to meet Professor Jordan to discuss with him the question of regulations. It is simply a matter of courtesy, which, I think, has been appreciated by the provincial governments in having these conferences before framing the regulations.

The reason I asked was because, last summer, there was a very deplorable condition of affairs on the Fraser river. Both the Dominion and provincial governments were attempting to enforce regulations, which regulations were conflicting in their terms, so that the Dominion government inserted in their licenses certain conditions for complying^ with which the provincial government carried the licenses into court, and vice versa.
And what was the result?
The matter is undeT appeal, I believe, and is expected to be argued in London in June.
What did the Supreme Court decide?
I am not a lawyer, and it is a very difficult thing for a layman to attempt to give a synopsis of a judicial decision.

I may tell the hon. gentleman what was done: We did pass regulations as a result of the British Columbia Commission, which were to be enforced last year. At the same time, I was surprised to hear that the provincial authorities though*

it advisable to issue licenses, to which they attached some regulations. The result was, as my hon. friend has stated, a conflict of jurisdiction which, I believe, must have created a great deal of dissatisfaction. But we were not to blame in that respect, because we acted within our rights and jurisdictions in providing those regulations. The matter was submitted to the courts, first a stipendiary magistrate, who upheld the action of the provincial authorities, and condemned the fishermen under the provincial regulations. This conviction was appealed to the county court which reserved the decision, declaring the regulations ultra vires, and that the licenses themselves, as a consequence, were illegal. An appeal was made by the provincial government to the High Court or Supreme Court of British Columbia, and I was glad to hear that the judgment of the magistrate of the county court was confirmed and the licenses were declared null and void. I am not aware that the case is appealed to the Privy Council. I am not surprised, however, because, when negotiations were entered into with the provincial government authorities and we tried to settle the conflict of jurisdiction, we were told that they intended to bring this question before the highest court in the realm. But I was not aware that the appeal had been made to the Privy Council.

That is my impression. I am speaking from newspaper report, but it has every appearance of correctness. I should have thought that the minister would try to reach a modus vivendi, so that there would not be a continuation of this state of things another year. Has any agreement been reached?

Unfortunately, we have not been able to reach such a conclusion. The provincial authorities claim that they have the absolute right to make regulations and issue licenses, and there was some talk that the matter should be submitted to the courts.
What is the condition of the law? Have the provincial government the right to issue licenses but not make regulations?
Yes.
And the Dominion government has power both to issue licenses and make regulations?

My reading of the judgment of the Privy Council is that the provincial governments have the right to issue licenses. It was formally enunciated in the judgment that the right to issue licenses existed also with the federal government. At the same time, we maintain that we are the only authority having the power to make regulations, and the judgment ren-Mr. BRODEUR.
dered by the court in British Columbia confirmed the position that we took on the question.
Do both governments have the right to insist on the payment of a fee in connection with the licenses?
Yes.
Have both governments, or rather both legislatures, the right to impose certain penalties if these licenses are not taken out?
Yes.
The hon. gentleman will understand that that is a point likely to lead to confusion.
Yes.

I have heard in this parliament for the last four years, or ever since that decision was rendered, that seme other question was to be submitted to the courts in order that the whole subject might be cleared up, and I have understood that negotiations have been going on from time to time to bring that about. But it seems to be very slow of consummation. It seems extremely desirable that so confusing a condition of affairs should be remedied at the earliest possible moment.

It is very unfortunate that this conflict of jurisdiction exists with regard to the fisheries, because I am quite ready to believe that it will have a bad effect upon our fisheries that we do not know exactly where we stand. The governments cannot act with the same interest as they would otherwise. Negotiations were held some years ago to submit to the court one of the questions raised, namely, whether the proprietary rights in the fisheries within the three-mile limit should be under the jurisdiction of the federal authority as maintained by this government. The question, however, was never submitted to the court. Another question was raised, also, whether the provincial authorities had the right to make regulations or the right to issue licenses and attach to those licenses conditions. In British Columbia, for example, there were conditions as to the fishing on Sunday. This was one of the questions submitted to the court, and the result was that the regulations made by the provincial authorities as to the fishing on Sunday were held to be illegal. A license should simply issue for the purpose of collecting fees, but it should not undertake in any way to regulate the manner in which the fisheries are carried on.
Was the subject taken up at the conference between this government and the provincial government some three years ago?
I do not know, I was not there at the time.

I was there, and the reason was this, that all the provinces were not interested in the question. The provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta were in no way interested, and as the interests of Ontario were different from those of the other provinces, it was thought better that the question should be left over for a further conference between the Dominion government and the provincial governments which were directly interested. I may be allowed further to say that the ground upon which it was held that the provinces could issue licenses was that they had a proprietary interest in the fisheries, and that therefore they had a right to say that no one should take fish except undeT license from the provincial government. But having a proprietary right was one thing, and the power to make regulations as to the mode and time of fishing was quite another; and the judicial committee held that, as a result, bcth governments can issue licenses, the provincial authorities simply giving the right to take property which belongs to the province, and the Dominion government having the right to regulate the fisheries under the provisions of the British North America Act, which expressly gives that power to the federal authority.
If that is the only result, it must be conceded that the fathers of confederation exercised a remarkable ingenuity in getting the whole subject into an extraordinary muddle.

For the information of the committee I may sa.y that the fishermen did not suffer iinancial loss last year on account of the double licenses, because it happened that the Dominion fee of $10 prevailing before last year was then reduced to $5, and the provincial fee then first in force, was also $5, so they only paid $10 the same as before. I referred just now to newspaper reports about taking this case to London, and I think the minister will be glad to learn of another newspaper report which is to the effect that for this season the provincial government proposes to accept the Dominion regulations and to issue licenses as a matter of collecting revenue only, and to make the licenses state on their face that they are subject to the Dominion regulations. I would ask the minister whether Professor Prince, when he goes west to meet Professor Starr Jordan at San Francisco, will go with carte blanche to make any arrangements he may think wise, or is he limited by instructions from the government?
I do not think it would be advisable to state what Professor Prince's instructions are.
Not the nature of the instructions, but whether there are any limitations.
I would not like to make any statement with Tegard to that. It is a matter of negotiation with the American commissioners, and I hope my hon. friend will not press for an answer.

I do not think we need to fight shadows. It is right the minister should not divulge what the instructions are, but there can be no harm in the minister telling us whether he has allowed this gentleman to go down there without instructions, or whether he has taken the precaution of giving him instructions; whether he has given him a line of conduct to pursue, or is letting him act of his own will. There is no state secret there. Parliament has a right to know whether the government has taken reasonable precautions that the rights of Canada shall not be sacrificed.

I would not like to make any statement with regard to that. Every hon. member who knows Professor Prince must feel confident that he would not sacrifice unduly the interests of Canada. _ If the government can give him instructions in the matter-because that is a point under the treaty,-I do not know whether it would be advisable for us to give him formal instructions. But I may assure my hon. friend that having due regard to the experience of Professor Prince, of his vast knowledge of the fisheries, and having regard also to his character, he will do nothing which will at all jeopardize the interests of our Canadian fisheries.

Could the minister tell us whether it is the federal or state authority that has the right to fix regulations on the inland lakes, as to size of nets, amount of fee, and territory to be covered by the license?

We are informed by the American authorities that the regulations with regard to fisheries on the boundary waters which are mentioned in the treaty, fall entirely under the control of the commissioners and of the federal authority. Formerly, all the regulations concerning fisheries were under the control of the state authorities, that was part of their jurisdiction under the constitution. But in virtue of another provision in the constitution, it is stated that the federal authority have the right to make treaties, and when those treaties are ratified by the Senate, they come into force and fall entirely under the control of the federal authority.
Could the minister say that by virtue of this treaty the right is taken away from the local authorities?

It is a very serious question my hon. friend is putting to me

when he asks me to interpret the constitution of the United States. If he will read the correspondence which is brought down he will find some letters from the Secretary of State for the United States to the effect that the federal authority has full power to regulate the fisheries under the treaty.

Is the minister relying entirely on the information given by the Attoney General of the United States; is he acting on the assumption that the local legislatures have no jurisdiction with reference to fixing the amount of the fee, the size of the net, the close season, and all matters pertaining to the fisheries? Is he accepting the opinion of the Attorney General of the United States as absolute with regard to those matters?

Well, I suppose we should not accept an opinion given by the Attorney General of the United States, but that we should accept the opinion which would be given here by our Department of Justice. If Mr. Root affirms the American central authorities have power to deal with that question we must assume that he is correct.
Has any intimation come from the local legislatures that they have agreed to that view of the law?
I do not know exactly what communications have been exchanged between the federal authorities and the state authorities.
Does the minister say now that these powers are being exercised by the local legislatures?
Formerly.
And now?
Not now.
They will until the regulations come into force?
Yes, of course.
Does the minister admit that the local legislatures in the Dominion have the power to fix the amount of the fee and require license for fishing?
We have always had the power to issue licenses. That power has not been taken from us but the provincial authorities have the same power too. That is the result of the judgment of the Privy Council.
Is it a fact that the provincial authorities now do fix the amount of the license fee in the Dominion?

Has the Dominion government the power to enforce a license and to fix a uniform amount as the license fee throughout the whole of the Dominion, or has each province the exclusive right to fix the amount of the fee?

In Ontario the local government issue licenses and fix the fees. While we have not formally exercised that power the federal authorities have the same power to issue licenses and to fix the fee for a license issued by the federal authorities.

Will it be possible for each state bordering on the Dominion of Canada to fix the amount of its license and likewise will it be possible for each province in the Dominion to fix the amount of its license?

As to the power of the states I am not familiar enough with their laws to say whether they will have a right to levy a fee upon their own fishermen. That is a matter, however, that does not concern us a great deal because each country preserves its absolute right to issue licenses on its own side of the water. If the state legislatures find it advisable to issue licenses and to levy taxes upon their own people that is a matter which does not concern us.

Will the minister advise me on this? Supposing that Professor Prince and the American Commissioner, while they are out in British Columbia, decide themselves upon these regulations, would this parliament then have any control over the matter or is the treaty not practically consummated r
The treaty provides for that. -
The treaty provides that if they come to an agreement this parliament has nothing to do at all with making the regulations ?

I am under the impression that there is a clause in the treaty providing that if any regulations are made the congress of the United States and the parliament of Canada will have authority

to take the necessary powers to carry out these regulations.
Then the minister can give us the assurance that we will have an opportunity of discussing these regulations later on ?
Yes, because they will have to be submitted to parliament to give the government or the commission the executive power which is required.

This is to pay the expenses in connection with the investigation of the Marine and Fisheries Department On the recommendation of Mr. Justice Cas-sels, $1,000 is to be paid Dr. Morse for his services in connection with the investigation, and upon the recommendation of counsel $300 is to be paid to Mr. H Thomas.
What is the total amount?

I understood the minister sometime ago to say, that, as he understood the treaty, once these representatives came to an agreement there was nothing for the congress of the United States or the Dominion parliament to do but accept the terms they had agreed to. He did not think we had the right to reject or revise it.

I suppose that if parliament should refuse to pass the necessary laws to carry out these regulations it would put an end to them ?
A Mn BRODEUR. It is estimated at $55,000, but we have not received all the ac counts. There was a vote of $15,000 last year.

Does Dr. Morse only get
$1,000?
He is an officer of the Exchequer Court and this is additional to his salary?
Will this vote pay all the expenses?
Yes.

I asked my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries some time ago if negotiations were on foot with the provincial governments with the view of adopting a modus vivendi respecting this conflict of jurisdiction but I do not think the minister understood my question. I was under the impression that some commission was appointed by the government to carry on negotiations. I would like to know what is being done.

We appointed, last year, a commissioner for the purpose of negotiating with the provincial authorities. Mr. Bastedo was the man who was selected for that purpose. The matter which was the most pressing at the time was the situation which arose in British Columbia and Mr. Bastedo communicated with the provincial authorities, made a visit or two and carried on negotiations with them. I must say that these negotiations were almost fruitless because immediately the provincial authorities decided to issue licenses themselves and in issuing their licenses they took it upon themselves to regulate to a certain extent, even to a very large extent, the fisheries. That, of course, made the question of jurisdiction more acute than it had been before. The matter was submitted _ to the courts and it was decided that the licenses issued under these conditions by the provincial authorities were null and void. I am informed by my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. J. lx Tavlor) that the question, though decided against the contention of the British Columbia government, is now being submitted to the Privy Council.
Marine and fisheries investigation-further amount required, $40,000.
I would like to ask the minister if he thinks this investigation was necessary?
I have no doubt it was.
What fees were paid counsel?

In a letter dated April 18, 1908, from the Minister of Justice to Mr. Watson, it is stated:-
With regard to your remuneration upon the inquiry before Mr. Justice Cassels, I have to confirm the understanding arrived at yesterday, that you would receive $100 per day and necessary expenses out of pocket, and m addition at the end of the investigation you would receive some further fee to be agreed upon having in view the responsibility involved in the inquiry and the magnitude it may assume.
Has that further fee been fixed?

The Minister of Justice informs me it has not.
To repay Cushing & Company amount deposited as security in connection with the seizure of the schooner ' Evolution ' in the year 1893 for alleged violation of shipping laws in Canada, $800.

But I want to say that if this ship cleared from St. John for the United States and found herself in Europe, how did she

If the Minister of Customs were here, or if anybody were here who knew about customs, he would know that, going to Santa Cruz, she would deposit $400 or $800, as the case may be, and that money would go into the customs and be handed over to the Receiver General. The government would not worry them about it, because the government would have the money, and if the owner wanted it back, he could make a demand for it.
He did make his demand; he made it fifteen years ago, and the matter was taken into the court.
If the hon. minister will wait until I get through, he will understand better
It will take some time.

It may take the minister some time, but it will not take other people so long. And perhaps a few people in the country will understand. Any one who knows anything about the customs law knows that there are dozens of cases every year of ships being seized for infractions jf the customs law and depositing $400 or $800 as the case may be, which money goes to the Receiver General, and even if they are guilty, the government does not worry themselves, because they have got the money, , and, so far as the government is concerned, the question is settled. The old government did many things that hon. gentlemen opposite said were wrong. Now, we want this government to do right. I have not had the honour of being here before, but now that I am here I want things to go right. I do not want to go back too far. ship cleared from St. John until she arrived in Europe. After she arrived in Europe, if she was there as a result of stress of weather, she would have to protest there and show the cause.
