I have heard enough to convince me that it is not fair to grant this money. Besides, in voting it, we should establish a precedent for every man who wanted to evade the customs law to clear his ship for a port where the law did not apply and to sail where he pleased. It will be unfair to the House and the country to pass this vote for various reasons which I do not wish to discuss at length. But I ask that the item shall be allowed to stand until we can get the papers before us to convince us that the circumstances were as these narties contend. If that is made clear, there will be nobody more ready than I to give Mr. Cushing all that is due him.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Crosby) is asking something that I cannot supply when he asks for the logbook.
I will put the hon minister in the way of getting that-if he does not know how, I can tell him.
These things happened fifteen years ago.
That does not matter.
For my part, I would be willing to receive the opinion of Mr. Justice Parker.
I do not know Mr. Justice Parker.

He was in charge of the case. He had to investigate the facts, and he reported thfit he was not able to reach a conclusion against the owners of the vessel. And, on the advice of the Department of Justice, and Mr. Justice Parker- Mr. Parker then, a lawyer-it was decided by the old government in 1896 to refund the money.
We have heard all that.

But my hon. friend (Mr. Crosby) is charging me with trying to do something which is unfair, so I desire to state the facts that have come to my knowledge. It was decided by the old government to reimburse these parties. Formal instructions were given by the Department of Marine to the Department of Customs to give back the money. The Department of Customs said that the money was not in their hands, and so it was found that an order in council was required. A recommendation to council, was prepared, but the elections came on and the orders in council were not



passed. After the case had been withdrawn, and after the formal undertaking of the government of Canada, I think we are bound to carry out the obligations of the former government, whether we disagree with them or not. I have been through these papers, and I shall be glad to bring them down, and the hon. member can satisfy himself that the case that was proceeded with for three years by the former government, when they decided tio repay the money, was gone on with in good faith, except that the formalities were not completed. It seems to me that it is only rendering justice to pay the claim under the circumstances. Whether the old government was right or wrong in prosecuting or not prosecuting that case is not the question. They decided not to prosecute but to abandon the case and pay the money. But the money was not paid, for the reasons I have given. To pay it under the circumstances would only be in accordance with justice.

The only argument the Minister of Marine and Fisheries puts up is that the old government recommended a let of appointments when they went out of power. If he was going to do all that the old government did when they went out of power, I could understand his argument. But I say that the log-book is available in every British ship, it is returned to the Trade Association in Great Britain, and the minister, or his department, is the collecting agency in Canada for that association. He can see the log-book or can if he wants to. He acts as the collection agency for the Board of Trade in London, and he can write and get that logbook any time he wants to. When he brings these papers here and shows what the Minister of Public Works indicates, then I will be satisfied. But we have no proof. It is no use for the Minister of Public Works to tell me that because this deposit was made, and because the government did not bring an action, this man had a right to go and ask for his deposit. There never was a case of that kind.
There is a regular proceeding for bringing the matter to court, and that was done in this case.
I beg the minister's pardon. I venture the assertion that when the Minister of Customs is here I will prove by him that that is not the case.
I have had dozens of cases in that way.

You may have had dozens of cases trying to get the money back for the man who put it in; but there has never been any case where the customs brought suit against a man after he had deposited his money; there was never a case where, after the money was deposited, the Minister of Customs or his officers brought suit against the man.

The proceeding is this: The notice is given by the Minister of Customs before the seizure. The owner is notified within so many days to put in a claim. He puts in a claim, and then the matter goes regularly to the Exchequer Court. The Crown is the plaintiff and the claimant is the defendant.

When the ship is seized and the sum is stated, it cannot be less than $400, the owner of the ship deposits his money. But there is no case on record, where after the money was deposited, the customs brought action against the man who deposited the money.
In this case, action had been taken by the government because it was for the payment of the penalty under the deck-load law.
What action did the government take?
An action for the penalty.
Did they take any action after they got the $800?
Yes, they took action for the recovery of the penalty provided under the deck-load law.
Didn't they have the penalty already?
No.
Then what are you going to get back if you have not got the penalty?

When there is a violation	of	a provision of	the
Shipping Act, and action has to be taken for the penalty provided by law, they immediately seize the vessel. Of course the vessel can be released, and it is done very often, on the deposit of a certain amount of money. That was ;done in this case, and then the action instituted by the Crown goes on, and has to be adjudicated. We often take action in my department against infractions of some of the provisions of the Shipping Act. In this case the government, after the case had been standing on the docket for three years, decided to withdraw the case and refund the money.

The minister says that he brought a case. Of course he did, he seized the ship. His case was good and he got the money. Now what more do you want? The other poor fellow is the one who has got a case. He had a hard case, and he couldn't get his money back for twelve years, and no wonder he is willing to get it back without interest.

I am acquainted with several cases of infractions of the customs law where a ship is seized; the own-

ers want to obtain a release and put.up a bond or a sum of money in order to obtain the release of the ship. Subsequently an action is taken, probably in the magistrate's court, to fix the penalty.

I would ask any man in this parliament if he ever knew a case in connection with the customs where an amount of money was deposited and action was brought, and the customs have got more than was deposited.

It is not a question of the violation of the customs laws, it is a question of the violation of the Shipping Act. The boat is seized, an action is taken by the Crown for the recovery of the penalty provided by the law, then the action goes on. In this case the action was withdrawn.
Who withdrew the action?
The government decided not to proceed with this case, and the Department of Marine and Fisheries gave instructions to the collector of customs to reimburse the money.
Bring these papers down and if they prove that the case is as the hon. minister has described it we will give the money, but until then 'I will vote against it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
For very many years an item of this character has been brought forward. It is a bookkeeping entry which the Auditor General desires for the closing up of his accounts. In some branches of the departments, it will be found that the grants have been greater than the expenditure, but in some other branches the expenditure is somewhat greater than the grant. In most instances the items are quite small, but occasionally they are quite considerable. The Auditor General desires to have this as bookkeeping entry. When we consider the vast current expenditure of the Dominion, this over expenditure of $200,000 or $300,000, scattered over all the departments, cannot be considered very large. With the best we can do, there will be occasionally some over expenditure.

When an expenditure is current, you cannot always tell what it will amount to. How can there be any possible reason why these items, at least for last year, should not have been passed in the supplementaries for last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course the government are responsible for everything, but as a matter of fact this is a book-keeping matter which the Auditor General sends in. The Auditor General asks for this whenever his accounts are finally adjusted. The current year is practically at an end and yet you cannot adjust these accounts for some weeks. Before they are adjusted it will be discovered that here and there are some large over-expenditures, but the amount in this case is not unusually large.
I see $162,000 in one department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is difficulty there; in the working of the Intercolonial Railway there may be quite large overexpenditures, but when you take a large service like the Intercolonial Railway the amount is not excessive.
This must have been known last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is the Auditor General who makes it known when he balances his accounts. It is his item particularly.
The first item is $29,000 for charges of management.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a large item, I have not the details here. My officials are not present.

That item was brought to the attention of the Auditor General later on when the accounts were being closed, but when the supplementaries were up the officers of the department must have known that this amount was going to be required to pay the Civil Service up to the 31st of March, last; but the estimates were not passed until May or June. Does the minister not think they should have had this in the supplementaries for last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is that the departmental estimates should have been made more closely ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the Finance Department this is not an over-expenditure, the law has provided for it by a permanent statute.
It seems to me the whole proceeding is illegal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, I suppose so.
Some resolutions reported.
On motion of Mr. Fielding House adjourned at 1 o'clock a.m. Saturday.

Monday, March 29, 1909.
